_meta.why_cached: The narrative layer is the only part of this prototype an LLM authored, and it is cached to disk on purpose. A live API call inside a ten-minute demo is a single point of failure for no benefit: the text does not change between runs unless the packages do. Scores and dispositions are never AI-generated — they come from the rulepack and can be replayed.
_meta.scope: Headline, decision and watch-out per package. Nothing here feeds back into scoring.

clean-core.headline: Six custom objects write directly into standard finance and sales document tables. That is seven write paths into the core you are trying to keep clean.
clean-core.decision: Remediate before conversion, or accept that the core is not clean on day one.
clean-core.watchOut: This one does not depend on usage evidence at all — the write paths are in the dependency extract whether or not anyone runs the code. It is the only package you can act on today without measuring anything first.

fork-live.headline: Eleven objects are running as forked pairs, and seven of them sit behind their own transaction code. Z_VENDOR_SCORECARD and Z_VENDOR_SCORECARD_V2 are both live — 1,229 and 2,515 executions a month, 71 and 58 users.
fork-live.decision: Resolve each fork before migrating either side. Otherwise the fork migrates too, and you pay to build both in S/4.
fork-live.watchOut: Two live versions usually means two groups of users with different expectations. The technical merge is the easy half.

fork-superseded.headline: Two predecessors whose successor is measurably carrying the load. Z_EDI_MAP_CUST01 still owns a transaction code while recording zero executions; its V2 runs 706 times a month with no transaction code of its own.
fork-superseded.decision: Retire the predecessor and repoint the transaction code at the successor.
fork-superseded.watchOut: Users are already reaching V2 somehow. Find out how before you move the transaction code, or you will break the path they actually use.

dead-clear.headline: Eleven custom objects measured at zero executions, with no transaction code and nothing calling them. Three independent signals agreeing.
dead-clear.decision: Retire as a batch. This is the strongest retirement case the extract supports.
dead-clear.watchOut: Confirm the extract spans a full business cycle. A year-end-only job measured over a quarter looks exactly like this.

dead-referenced.headline: Four objects measured at zero executions that something still points at — two of them behind live transaction codes.
dead-referenced.decision: Investigate before retiring. Dead code with a live entry point is a governance question, not a cleanup task.
dead-referenced.watchOut: Either the transaction is genuinely unused and should go with the code, or the measurement is wrong. Both answers matter, and they lead to different places.

workshop.headline: Five business-critical custom objects, every one behind its own transaction code and actively used. The business reaches these directly.
workshop.decision: Book the fit-to-standard workshop. Each must exist on the other side in some form — the question is whether S/4 standard covers it.
workshop.watchOut: Metadata cannot tell you whether standard covers a custom function. This scopes the workshop; it does not pre-empt it.

tables.headline: Eighteen custom tables, and usage.csv covers none of them — zero of thirty-two tables in the whole extract. Execution semantics do not apply to tables, so the usual evidence simply is not there. Fifteen are read or written by something; three are touched by nothing at all.
tables.decision: These carry data, so they are the pivot in a selective transition: what moves is decided by which tables follow which slice.
tables.watchOut: The evidence here is read and write access from the dependency extract alone. The three untouched tables look like free retirements and are not — no reads in a dependency extract is not the same as no rows in the database. Get row counts and last-change timestamps first.

migration-residue.headline: Eight objects left over from the 2011 migration with no evidence of use. The migration-era packages hold thirty-four objects in total; the rest are demonstrably still working and are decided on their own merits.
migration-residue.decision: Measure these, then retire as a batch. One decision, taken once.
migration-residue.watchOut: Fifteen years is long enough for a migration helper to quietly become a business process. Measure before you batch.

unmeasured-referenced.headline: Six objects with no usage row that something still references — two are reachable from a transaction code.
unmeasured-referenced.decision: Hold. Nothing here should be retired on the evidence available.
unmeasured-referenced.watchOut: This is the package that punishes a confident tool. Absence of measurement is not absence of use, and these are exactly the objects a single-criterion orphan test would have deleted.

unmeasured-candidates.headline: Two objects with no usage row, no callers and no path from any transaction code. Three weak signals agreeing — which is not the same as one strong one.
unmeasured-candidates.decision: Measure them, then retire. These are the strongest retirement candidates in the extract and they are still not retirements.
unmeasured-candidates.watchOut: This is the package that tempts a tool into overreach. Every signal here is an absence, and absence of measurement is not absence of use. Measuring costs one collection window; getting it wrong costs a business process.

carry.headline: Thirty-three custom objects running measurably but with no transaction code — reached by batch, interface or RFC. Used, but not business entry points.
carry.decision: Carry forward. No signal argues otherwise.
carry.watchOut: Being invisible to the transaction list is not the same as being unused. These would look like orphans to any tool that only checks transaction codes.
